title: [review] results/cab6-packing: cited exact Q(sqrt2) all-pairs check is not in the repository and the referee is unnamed
body:
## Which result and commit

- Result folder: `results/cab6-packing`
- Commit reviewed: `db3b51d` (main)
- Statement or step in question: the evidence cited for the PROVEN attainment label, `results/cab6-packing/PROOF.md:3`:
  > attainment and all-pairs non-overlap PROVEN (exact classification of every pair over the whole lattice, [ATTAINMENT.md](ATTAINMENT.md); referee-checked, an exact all-pairs check in Q(sqrt2) agreed)

The proof in `ATTAINMENT.md` is not in question. Two things around it are wrong. First, the exact Q(sqrt2) all-pairs check cited as agreeing evidence is not in the repository, so nobody can replay it. Second, the referee is not named. The fix needs a decision from the maintainer, because only the maintainer knows whether the check's code still exists and who the referee was.

## Kind of finding

- [ ] Mathematical error or gap in a proof
- [ ] A finite check does not support the stated claim (range, tolerance or hypothesis too weak)
- [ ] The replay fails or the certificate changes (`make verify`, Python version, platform)
- [ ] Prior art that the repository does not cite
- [ ] Label is too strong or too weak (PROVEN / VERIFIED / KNOWN)
- [x] Other: a check cited as evidence for a PROVEN label is not in the repository and cannot be replayed, and the reviewer is not named (ledger rule 5). The replay that does exist passes, and no label or value is wrong.

## Evidence

### 1. Where the check is cited

| Location | Text |
|---|---|
| `results/cab6-packing/PROOF.md:3` | "referee-checked, an exact all-pairs check in Q(sqrt2) agreed" |
| `results/cab6-packing/ATTAINMENT.md:3` | "Status: **PROVEN** (written proof; internal referee review, with an exact all-pairs check in Q(sqrt2) in agreement; independent human review pending)" |
| `docs/review-ledger.md:25` (PR #23 row) | "a referee confirmed it correct and complete, and an exact all-pairs check in Q(sqrt2) agreed. Attainment upgraded from VERIFIED to PROVEN. Exact radical checks, 966 translated B-B pairs and 936 (h, gamma) comparisons corroborate it" |
| `open.html:154` | "Referee-checked: an exact all-pairs check in Q(√2) agreed. Internal review only; independent human review pending." |

Some places cite the referee without the Q(sqrt2) check:
- `open.html:111`: "internal referee review"
- `index.html:274`: "referee-checked, with human review pending"
- the evidence label at `tools/build_certificates.py:44`, which is generated into `certificates/selected-results.json:52`: "internal referee review, human review pending"

### 2. The check is not in the repository

```
$ git ls-files results/cab6-packing
results/cab6-packing/ATTAINMENT.md
results/cab6-packing/PROOF.md
results/cab6-packing/cab6_packing.py
results/cab6-packing/certificate.json
results/cab6-packing/verify.py

$ git grep -nIwE '966|936' db3b51d
db3b51d:docs/review-ledger.md:25:| [PR #23](...) | cab6-packing | ...   <- the citation itself
db3b51d:fold-path.js:3:window.FOLDPATH={"n":793,"dens":[...         <- unrelated numeric data
db3b51d:research/chemistry/cod/2103136.cif:96:_exptl_absorpt_coefficient_mu    15.966
```

`results/cab6-packing` has never held any file other than these five in any of the 35 commits reachable from `db3b51d`. The PR #23 squash commit `eaf6274` adds only `ATTAINMENT.md` to that folder. A read-only look through the GitHub API shows that the three commits on the PR #23 branch (`4b728d4`, `8fe316b`, `8252530`) add no script or output either, and PR #23 has no comments and no reviews.

### 3. What `make verify-cab6` replays

`Makefile:51-52` runs only `results/cab6-packing/verify.py`.
- **Exact part** (`verify.py:4`, `:32-65`): checks the closed form, the optimum h*, the fcc window ends and a single Ca-B distance. For that distance, `verify.py:41-43` takes `dCaB = sp.sqrt(x ** 2 + 1/2)` and tests the gap after `sp.N(..., 12)`.
- **Pair checks:** all of them come from the floating-point brute force in `cab6_packing.py` over a 5 x 5 x 5 block (`cab6_packing.py:40`, `:51-59`; `verify.py:5-6`).
- **Certificate:** `certificate.json` records no exact all-pairs counts. Its `exact` block holds the closed form, h*, x, the Ca-B gap and the fcc window. Its brute-force block says `"cell_block": "5x5x5, all pairs"`.

Run in a clean worktree at `db3b51d`:

```
$ make verify-cab6 PY=.../python
.../python results/cab6-packing/verify.py
cab6-packing: OK (max |brute - closed| < 1e-9 on 15 ratios; 6 controls rejected)
$ git status --short        # empty: certificate.json unchanged
```

### 4. Where the wording and the counts come from (PR #23 history, read-only GitHub API)

- **The 966/936 sentence came first.** It was in the ledger row from the PR's first commits (`4b728d4`, link fixed in `8fe316b`), when the row's verdict was still `open`. It repeats the Validation item in the PR #23 description: "Exact radical identities, 966 translated B-B pairs, and 936 `(h, gamma)` comparisons corroborate the argument; maximum formula difference was at most 5.56e-16. These finite checks are corroboration, not the proof." A maximum difference of 5.56e-16 suggests that at least the (h, gamma) comparisons were done in floating point, but the ledger now groups them under "Exact radical checks".
- **The referee wording came later.** `8252530` ("Merge main; upgrade CaB6 attainment from VERIFIED to PROVEN", with a `Co-Authored-By` trailer for a Claude model) did the following:
  - changed the row's verdict to "confirmed (internal); outside review open";
  - added "a referee confirmed it correct and complete, and an exact all-pairs check in Q(sqrt2) agreed";
  - wrote `PROOF.md:3` and `ATTAINMENT.md:3` in their current form.

  The commit names no referee and adds no check.

So the tree cites up to two checks that are not recorded anywhere: the PR author's finite checks (the 966/936 counts) and the referee's Q(sqrt2) check. They may or may not be the same check.
- **966:** this is 6·6·27 − 6, the number of ordered B-B pairs from the six B sites of one cell to all B sites in the 27 cells with translates in [-1,1]^3 (the probe below reproduces it). That hints at the enumeration that was used.
- **936:** nothing in the repository reproduces it. In the probe's [-1,1]^3 enumeration, 966 − 30 = 936 pairs are not contacts. The record cannot tell whether that is what the "936 (h, gamma) comparisons" were.

### 5. The referee is not named

- `docs/review-ledger.md:25` says only "a referee confirmed it".
- Rule 5 at `docs/review-ledger.md:36` says: "Say who reviewed and whether AI tools were used."
- Other rows do name their reviewers, for example `:11` ("implementation by GPT-6.1 Sol, reviewed by GPT-6") and `:24` ("Internal AI review by GPT-6 and GPT-6.1 Sol").
- `papers/source/main.tex:381` says "All reviews so far were performed by AI models under direction; no person other than the author has checked the proofs", so the referee was presumably an AI model. Which one is not recorded anywhere.
- `ATTAINMENT.md:106` and `CONTRIBUTORS.md:23` credit only GPT-6 (the proof) and GPT-6 Luna (the submission).

### 6. The claim itself stands

The audit re-read the lemma (`ATTAINMENT.md:16-42`) and the five-contact classification (`:90-96`) and found them correct. `ATTAINMENT.md:100-101` already says that finite replay "corroborates the result but is not the justification for the infinite-lattice claim". An independent sympy probe written for this audit (not in the repository) agrees with the proof:

```
translates [-1,1]^3: ordered B-B pairs 966, B-B contacts 30, B-B non-contacts 936, Ca-B contacts 0, violations 0, min dCaB^2-(rL+rS)^2 = 3/4 - sqrt(2)/2 = 0.0428932
translates [-2,2]^3: ordered B-B pairs 4494, B-B contacts 30, B-B non-contacts 4464, Ca-B contacts 0, violations 0, min dCaB^2-(rL+rS)^2 = 3/4 - sqrt(2)/2 = 0.0428932
```

<details><summary>Probe script (sympy; central-cell B sites against Ca and B in the translates)</summary>

```python
import itertools, sympy as sp
s2 = sp.sqrt(2)
h = 1 - s2/2            # offset of B from the octahedron centre (1/2,1/2,1/2); Wyckoff x = 1/2 - h
rL = sp.Rational(1, 2)
rS = (s2 - 1)/2
half = sp.Rational(1, 2)
B = []
for m in range(3):
    for sg in (1, -1):
        p = [half]*3; p[m] += sg*h; B.append(p)
def d2(p, q): return sp.expand(sum((a-b)**2 for a, b in zip(p, q)))
def run(R):
    sh = list(itertools.product(range(-R, R+1), repeat=3))
    bb = cab = viol = pairs_bb = 0; mins = []
    for b in B:
        for n in sh:
            ca = list(n)
            dd = d2(b, ca); diff = sp.nsimplify(sp.expand(dd - (rL+rS)**2))
            if diff == 0: cab += 1
            if (diff < 0) == True: viol += 1
            mins.append(diff)
            for q in B:
                qq = [q[i]+n[i] for i in range(3)]
                if qq == b: continue
                pairs_bb += 1
                diffb = sp.expand(d2(b, qq) - (2*rS)**2)
                if diffb == 0: bb += 1
                if (diffb < 0) == True: viol += 1
    m = min(mins, key=lambda e: float(e))
    print(f"translates [-{R},{R}]^3: ordered B-B pairs {pairs_bb}, B-B contacts {bb}, B-B non-contacts {pairs_bb-bb}, Ca-B contacts {cab}, violations {viol}, min dCaB^2-(rL+rS)^2 = {sp.simplify(m)} = {float(m):.7f}")
run(1); run(2)
```

</details>

## Suggested fix or follow-up

The maintainer needs to decide. Neither option changes a label, a value or a certificate number.

1. **Option A (preferred): commit an exact check.**
   - If the referee's Q(sqrt2) script, or the script behind the 966/936 counts, still exists, commit it and reproduce its counts exactly.
   - Otherwise add `results/cab6-packing/exact_pairs.py`, run from `verify.py`. It should:
     - use sympy at h* = 1 − sqrt2/2, rL = 1/2, rS = (sqrt2 − 1)/2 (gamma* = sqrt2 − 1);
     - compare the six central-cell B sites with every Ca and B site in the translates [-2,2]^3;
     - assert 30 ordered B-B contacts (5 per B), 0 Ca-B contacts, 0 violations, and min d_CaB^2 − (rL + rS)^2 = 3/4 − sqrt2/2;
     - decide the sign of each a + b·sqrt2 exactly (for example by comparing a^2 with 2b^2), not by numerical evaluation.
   - Record the counts in `certificate.json`, then run `make certificates` to regenerate `certificates/` and `commitment/`.
   - This edits `verify.py`, so it needs its own checker PR. #59 also edits `verify.py` and `cab6_packing.py` and regenerates the same certificate. Merge one of the two, rebase the other, and regenerate once.
   - `docs/audit.md:61` can then list the exact check next to the brute force; #66 also edits that line.
   - The new check is still finite corroboration. `ATTAINMENT.md` stays the proof.
2. **Option B: reword the citation in a docs-only PR.**
   - At `PROOF.md:3`, `ATTAINMENT.md:3`, `docs/review-ledger.md:25` and `open.html:154`, use wording such as "an exact Q(sqrt2) all-pairs check run during internal review (not committed) agreed".
   - In `docs/review-ledger.md:25`, also say that the 966/936 checks were run for PR #23 and not committed. Drop "exact" for the (h, gamma) comparisons unless they really were exact.
   - Expect small conflicts: #66 edits `PROOF.md:3`, and #65 edits `open.html`.
3. **With either option, name the referee.**
   - Name the referee (model and version, or person) in `docs/review-ledger.md:25`, as rows `:11` and `:24` do, and say what the referee did: re-derived the classification, ran the Q(sqrt2) check, or both.
   - #80 also edits this row and `ATTAINMENT.md:106` to record `8252530`; combine the two wordings.
   - The short labels at `open.html:111`, `index.html:274` and `tools/build_certificates.py:44` do not mention Q(sqrt2). They can either name the referee or keep "internal referee review" and rely on the ledger as the record. A change to `build_certificates.py:44` requires `make certificates`.
   - Related: #39.
4. Add a ledger row for the follow-up PR; see #41.

Questions for the maintainer:
- (a) Does the referee's Q(sqrt2) check, or the script behind the 966/936 counts, still exist?
- (b) Who, or which model and version, was the referee?
- (c) Option A or option B?

title: RS Oph, March to April 1914: check the flag

labels.name: task
labels.description: One piece of work, with what done means and how it is checked

body:
### What to do

Decide whether the bright RS Oph plates of March and April 1914 show a real eruption.

- Inspect the plate images around RS Oph for every plate from 13 February to 25 May 1914.
- Check DASCH's quality flags on each plate.
- Rule out an asteroid with [SkyBoT](https://vo.imcce.fr/webservices/skybot/), a service that lists the known asteroids near a position at a given time.
- Check stars of similar brightness near RS Oph on the same plates. If they also look too bright, the plate is at fault.

### Done when

A note in `results/` with the plate list, a cutout of the image around RS Oph from each plate, the quality flags, the SkyBoT result, the check of neighbouring stars, and a verdict: eruption, plate fault, or undecided.

### How the result is checked

Someone else fetches the same cutouts and gets the same measurements. A person looks at the images and signs before any claim is made.

### Context

- The pilot's test flags three plates of 20, 21 and 25 March 1914 (series `ai`, magnitude 8.45 to 8.74, against a median of 11.24). Four more plates up to 18 April show the star at 9.5 to 9.8. The plate list is at the end of [results/pilot-2026-10-19.txt](https://github.com/Foundation-0/plate-novae/blob/main/results/pilot-2026-10-19.txt).
- Against an eruption: star images on the `ai` plates are about 2′ across. On five of the six `ai` plates the star lies 26 to 28 degrees from the plate centre. DASCH rejects two of the seven plates, and the stricter quality mask of plate-eclipses drops three more.
- No 1914 eruption appears in the literature the scouting found, and Schaefer has searched these plates (from the scouting report, not yet re-checked). An eruption is unlikely.
- plate-eclipses fetches and re-measures plate cutouts in [src/cutouts.py](https://github.com/Foundation-0/plate-eclipses/blob/main/src/cutouts.py) and [src/remeasure.py](https://github.com/Foundation-0/plate-eclipses/blob/main/src/remeasure.py).

title: Make the matcher catch transposed copies and small variants, and measure what that adds

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: task
labels.description: One piece of work, with what done means and how it is checked

body:
### What to do

The pilot only finds exact copies: the same 12 pitches, at the same height. Extend the matcher in two steps, and measure what each step adds:

1. Match by the steps between notes rather than the notes themselves, so that a copy written in another key (a transposed copy) also matches.
2. Allow small differences, such as one changed note or one repeated note.

For each step, estimate how many of the new matches are chance, for example by checking a sample by hand or by matching against shuffled incipits.

### Done when

`results/<date>.md` gives counts by genre for exact, transposed and near matches, with the estimate of chance matches for each.

### How the result is checked

The new script runs on the same export as the pilot (its SHA-1 is in [results/pilot-2026-10-19.md](https://github.com/Foundation-0/rism-anon/blob/main/results/pilot-2026-10-19.md)). Its exact-match counts must equal the pilot's.

### Context

The pilot takes the first 12 pitches of each incipit, needs at least 5 different pitches, and ignores rhythm. Shared tunes, such as chorales, already match often, so near matches are likely to add the most noise there.

title: Calibrate the eruption test on the 10 known Galactic recurrent novae

labels.name: task
labels.description: One piece of work, with what done means and how it is checked

body:
### What to do

Run the eruption test on the DASCH light curves of the 10 known Galactic recurrent novae. For each known eruption from about 1890 to 1990, record:

- how many plates DASCH has in the 60 days after it starts;
- the outcome: recovered (at least 3 plates from at least 2 plate series), single plate, or missed.

Then give the recovery rate against plate coverage.

Also settle how to set each star's quiet level. The pilot found that the median of a star's measurements is too bright for stars that DASCH sees mostly in eruption. With the median, U Sco's 1936 eruption shows on one plate. With the star's catalogue magnitude, it shows on 6 plates from 4 series.

### Done when

- A table in `results/` with one row per eruption: star, date, plates in the 60 days after it, outcome.
- The recovery rate, for all eruptions and for those with plates in the 60 days after them.
- The code that makes the table, and the quiet-level rule it uses.

### How the result is checked

Anyone can re-run the committed code on freshly fetched light curves and get the same table. Each eruption date cites its source.

### Context

- Pilot: 5 of 17 eruptions of T Pyx, U Sco and RS Oph recovered with the median quiet level, 6 of 17 with catalogue magnitudes. Four of the misses fall in 1953–69, when Harvard took few plates. See [results/pilot-2026-10-19.txt](https://github.com/Foundation-0/plate-novae/blob/main/results/pilot-2026-10-19.txt).
- Schaefer's "Comprehensive Photometric Histories of All Known Galactic Recurrent Novae" ([arXiv:0912.4426](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.4426)) is the starting point for the list of eruptions. Not yet re-checked.
- Be gentle with the DASCH API: fetch in small batches and cache results.

labels.name: task

### What to do

title: Write the equations and symmetry reduction in NOTE.md, with the exponent as a parameter

labels.name: good first issue
labels.description: Good for newcomers

labels.name: task
labels.description: One piece of work, with what done means and how it is checked

body:
### What to do

[NOTE.md](https://github.com/Foundation-0/relative-equilibria/blob/main/NOTE.md) has a first draft of the equations for planar central configurations, with the exponent `a` as a parameter (`a = 1` for gravity, `a = 0` for vortices), and of the symmetries to remove (translation, rotation, scaling, relabelling). Check the draft and complete Section 3:

- Choose how to fix translation, rotation and scale, and which three equations to drop. Show that the remaining equations imply the dropped ones everywhere in the search region.
- State and prove bounds that make the search region compact: a lower bound on the distance between any two bodies in a solution, and an upper bound on the size once the scale is fixed, both as functions of `a`.
- Say how classes are counted when only part of the region is searched because of the relabelling symmetry.

### Done when

Sections 1 to 3 of NOTE.md give a square reduced system and a compact search region, with a proof or a reference for every step, and no open points left.

### How the result is checked

A second contributor re-derives the reduced system and the bounds, and confirms them on the pull request. A numerical solve of the reduced system for 3 equal masses, from many random starting points, finds the classical solutions (Lagrange's equilateral triangle and Euler's collinear configurations) and nothing else.

### Context

- How point-charges bounded its search region: Section 4 of its [NOTE.md](https://github.com/Foundation-0/point-charges/blob/main/NOTE.md).
- Moczurad and Zgliczyński certified the full lists for 5, 6 and 7 equal masses ([arXiv:1812.07279](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.07279)).

### Done when

Both checkers, their tests and the workflow are merged, and the workflow passes on main. README.md has a "Check it yourself" section with the commands.

### How the result is checked

Both checkers accept the known covering systems in the tests and reject the near misses, such as a known system with one congruence removed. Anyone can run the commands in README.md and see the same.

### Context

- A list covers every integer exactly when it covers every remainder on division by the lcm, the least common multiple of its moduli. For record systems the lcm is too large to try every remainder. The scouting report suggests working through the lcm's prime factors with the Chinese remainder theorem instead (not yet re-checked).

title: Solar systems and galaxies: where Kepler's law holds, where rotation curves go flat, and the little solar system at the Galaxy's centre

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
## Question

The README opens with "atoms look a little like solar systems, solar systems a little like galaxies". The first half of that line has a study (the Witness Map). The second half has none.

A solar system and a spiral galaxy are both flattened, rotating disks, but they orbit differently:
- **The Solar System.** The Sun holds about 99.86% of the mass, so orbital speeds fall as Kepler's v ∝ r^−1/2.
- **The Milky Way.** The circular speed stays near 230 km/s from about 5 to 25 kpc (Eilers et al. 2019, as recalled), so the mass enclosed grows roughly ∝ r.

Where does each law hold, and what sets the boundary? Can one small model show both regimes and where one turns into the other?

## First estimates

These numbers come from a scoping script and from recall. Check them before they go into a README or a test.

- **Where the Sun's Kepler law ends.** It ends at the Sun's tidal (Jacobi) radius in the Galaxy, r_J = [GM☉ / (4A(A − B))]^(1/3). With Oort constants A = 15.3 and B = −11.9 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹ (Bovy 2017), this gives 1.37 pc, about 2.8×10⁵ AU, near the Oort cloud's outer edge.
- **The Galaxy's own Kepler region.** Inside Sgr A*'s sphere of influence, r_h = GM_BH/σ², which is about 1.8 pc for σ = 100 km/s, stars orbit the way planets do.
  - Take GRAVITY's 2020 elements for S2: a = 125.058 mas, P = 16.0455 yr, e = 0.8846, R₀ = 8246.7 pc.
  - Kepler's third law then returns 4.26×10⁶ M☉. That is their fitted mass, so this is a consistency check, not a measurement.
  - General relativity's precession formula gives 12.1′ per orbit. They detected 12′.
  - So the analogy holds within about 2 pc of the Galaxy's centre, about the same reach as the Sun's own Kepler law, and fails across the disk.
- **The missing mass in one line.** Treat the baryons, about 6×10¹⁰ M☉, as a point mass. That gives 177 km/s at R₀ and 102 km/s at 25 kpc, against about 230 measured.
- **How exact Kepler is in the Solar System.** From JPL's approximate mean elements (1800–2050), n²a³ matches the IAU GM☉ to about 0.1%.
  - Jupiter's and Saturn's residuals are close to their own masses.
  - Uranus's and Neptune's residuals, about 1×10⁻³, are closer to the mass of the planets inside their orbits.
  - A test should model both effects (and say which frame the elements are in) before it claims a tolerance.
- **An acceleration scale.** In galaxies the empirical crossover is an acceleration: g† ≈ 1.2×10⁻¹⁰ m s⁻² in the radial acceleration relation (McGaugh, Lelli and Schombert 2016).
  - The Sun's own pull falls to g† at about 7,000 AU, inside its tidal radius.
  - Wide-binary tests at those separations disagree (Chae 2023 against Banik et al. 2024), so the study should report this as contested and not build on it.

## What does repeat

Flattened, rotating disks appear at both scales, because gas loses energy but keeps its angular momentum. The planets' orbits are inclined by a few degrees. The Galaxy's thin disk has a height-to-length ratio of about 0.1. A short paragraph, with sources, is enough.

## First steps

- [ ] `orbits/model.js`, covering:
  - Kepler's third law, with the planet's own mass and the interior-mass corrections;
  - the Jacobi radius;
  - S2's orbit and its precession;
  - a Milky Way mass model with Sgr A* added. For example, Bovy's MWPotential2014 (power-law bulge with a cutoff, Miyamoto–Nagai disk, NFW halo). It should give v(r) from 10⁻³ pc to 100 kpc and the log slope d ln v / d ln r.
- [ ] Mark where that slope is −1/2 and where it is near 0. The boundary should come out as a ratio of enclosed mass to central mass, not a fixed size.
- [ ] Check against:
  - the IAU 2015 nominal GM☉ and JPL's elements;
  - GRAVITY 2020 (S2);
  - Eilers et al. 2019 (the flat curve and its gradient of about −1.7 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹);
  - Bovy 2017 (the Oort constants).
- [ ] Say what this does not settle. Dark matter against modified gravity is the Witness Map's and #3's ground. This study only measures where the Keplerian nesting stops.

body:
The float64 certifier does not finish on the seven-charge configuration $C_7$ (`certificates/n7-abk-second-pair.json`, built by `explore/second_pair.py`).

Observed on 18 Oct 2026 (Mac, Python 3.12, numpy 2.5.4), certifying $C_7$ directly with `certify.run`:

- Default budget: `RuntimeError: box budget exceeded` after 5,000,000 boxes in 37 s.
- Raised budget (`max_boxes=60_000_000`): process killed after a peak memory footprint of about 53 GB, with no certificate written. The breadth-first queue and its `(m, n, 3)` intermediates grow without bound.

For comparison, the independent verifier proves $C_7$ completely: 44 Krawczyk boxes plus a completeness subdivision of 394,265 boxes in about 71 s. Its Arb mean-value enclosures exclude far earlier than the float64 enclosures near the second cluster, whose smallest Hessian eigenvalue is about $5\times10^{-7}$.

Wanted: make `certify.py` reproduce the $C_7$ count within ordinary resources (say under 4 GB and a few minutes), without weakening any enclosure. Directions: bound memory by processing the queue in chunks (depth-first batches reusing the existing kernels); attempt Krawczyk more selectively near near-degenerate zeros; or reduce enclosure overestimation near the centre. Acceptance: `make_certs.py`-style regeneration of $C_7$ (44, indices 19/25), `verify_arb.py` passes on the result, and $C_3$ to $C_6$ still regenerate and verify.

title: Open problem: configurations beating (n−1)² equilibria for eight or more charges

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
Every known construction grows linearly in n, while Maxwell's bound grows quadratically. So the bound is now known to fail only for n = 5, 6, 7:

| n | Maxwell | best known | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 16 | 24 | Arathoon, Ball, Kvalheim (arXiv:2607.27197) |
| 6 | 25 | 29 | this repository |
| 7 | 36 | 44 | ABK Proposition 1 |
| 8 | 49 | 49 (tie) | ABK Proposition 1 + `NOTE.md` Proposition 2 (sketch, not certified) |
| 9 | 64 | 64 (tie) | ABK Proposition 1 |
| ≥ 10 | (n−1)² | about 10n | below the bound |

## Questions
- Is there a construction with superlinear growth: clusters of clusters, lattices, or many charges near a highly degenerate critical point?
- Can n = 8 be pushed to 50 or more? That would be the first counterexample above seven charges.
- Edelsbrunner, Fillmore and Oliveira ask a related question about unit charges (ratio above 25/7).

title: Open problem: computer-assisted proof of Maxwell's bound for three charges

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Extra attention is needed

body:
For three positive charges the maximum number of equilibria is 4 or 6:
- at most 6 by Gabrielov, Novikov, Novikov and Shapiro (arXiv:2607.28785, July 2026);
- 4 for equal charges (Tsai, Physica D 2015) and in other special cases (Tsai, Nonlinearity 2011).

Maxwell's bound of 4 is equivalent to "at most one local minimum of the in-plane potential".

## Reformulation (`NOTE.md` §3)
For a triangle A₁A₂A₃ and an interior point x there is exactly one charge ratio making x an equilibrium (Lami's theorem):

  ζᵢ = rᵢ² wᵢ,  (w₁ : w₂ : w₃) = (u₂×u₃ : u₃×u₁ : u₁×u₂).

The folds of the map Z: x ↦ [ζ(x)] are exactly the degenerate equilibria. Maxwell's bound for that triangle is equivalent to **Z being one-to-one on R_min = {det Hess > 0}**.

## Evidence so far
`explore/three_scan.py` scanned 1,289 triangle shapes.
- In the 799 shapes where R_min is resolved, no charge ratio was covered twice. Three flagged pixels were re-solved directly and are artifacts (`results/three_scan_summary.txt`).
- In the other 487 shapes, mostly very flat triangles, no minimum region showed up at grid resolution.

## Possible plan
1. Prove injectivity of Z on R_min with interval arithmetic over compact boxes of triangle shapes. One route: show Z is injective on ∂R_min and use degree theory. Another: show det DZ has a fixed sign plus a covering argument.
2. Handle the non-compact ends separately by asymptotics: flat triangles and charge ratios going to 0 or ∞.
3. A proof on a compact part of the parameter space would already be a publishable partial result.

title: Open problem: can four point charges have more than 9 equilibria?

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Extra attention is needed

body:
Maxwell's bound for four charges is (4−1)² = 9. It is known to fail for five, six and seven charges, and is attained for four (`certificates/n4-triangle-plus-centre.json`). Is 9 the maximum for four positive charges?

## What we know
- With non-degenerate equilibria, #equilibria = 3 + 2·m₁, where m₁ counts 1-saddles. More than 9 means m₁ ≥ 4.
- **Inverse map.** For a fixed tetrahedron, each interior point x is an equilibrium for exactly one charge ray. Maxwell's bound for that tetrahedron is equivalent to the map x ↦ charges covering the index-1 region at most three times.
- **Searches** (`results/SUMMARY.md`), none of which found more than 9:
  - fine scans of the C₃ᵥ family (triangle plus one axial charge);
  - random multi-scale sampling;
  - ghost-guided hill climbing;
  - importance sampling through the inverse map (16,179 charge vectors);
  - a least-squares search for four 1-saddles sharing one charge vector. It never converged; its best runs flatten the tetrahedron.
- **Local models.** One small charge in a smooth background creates at most 4 nearby equilibria, or 6 when the background is axially symmetric. So "three charges plus one" designs stop at 9.

## Ways forward
- **Refute:** a design that is not "three plus one". Two pairs at different scales? Near-coplanar limits, where the least squares drifts?
- **Prove:** a computer-assisted argument over the 5-parameter shape space using the inverse map. It needs an analysis of degenerate (flat or elongated) tetrahedra.
- Either outcome is a real result. Any configuration found should be certified with `certify.py` and `verify_arb.py`.

title: Halos within halos: how deep does the nesting go, and does the dark matter particle set the floor?

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
## Question

In cold dark matter simulations, halos sit inside halos with nearly the same shape from about an Earth mass up to galaxy clusters, some 20 decades in mass (Wang et al., Nature 585, 39 (2020), arXiv:1911.09720). The nesting has to stop at a smallest halo, and the particle sets it:

- For a ~100 GeV WIMP, the floor is set at kinetic decoupling, by acoustic damping and free streaming: about 10⁻⁶ M☉ for a typical bino (Green, Hofmann and Schwarz 2004; Diemand, Moore and Stadel, Nature 433, 389 (2005)). Across WIMP models it spans several decades, roughly 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻³ M☉ (Bringmann 2009, as recalled).
- For wave dark matter, the floor is the quantum-pressure (Jeans) scale (Hu, Barkana and Gruzinov, PRL 85, 1158 (2000)).

Can a small model derive both floors and count how many levels of nesting a Milky Way holds in each case?

## Why it matters

It is the repository's question ("where does the repetition stop, and why") asked of dark matter itself, and it connects to the first study.

- **The Jeans scale in Witness Map terms.** The Jeans condition can be rewritten with the wave clock: with k_J⁴ = 16πGρm²/ħ², the wave clock at Δx = 1/k_J is m/(ħk_J²) = 1/(4√(πGρ)). That is a restatement of the Jeans criterion, not a coincidence, and the factor depends on convention: with Δx = λ_J/2 the ratio is π² instead of 1.
- **How many levels of nesting.** A first estimate gives about 18 decades for a 100 GeV WIMP and only 2 to 4.5 for 10⁻²² eV wave dark matter. But 10⁻²² eV is the mass the lensing thread uses (#1, #11), and it is excluded by Lyman-α and Milky Way satellite bounds (from about 2×10⁻²¹ to 3×10⁻¹⁹ eV, depending on the probe; all assume wave dark matter is all of the dark matter). At 2×10⁻²⁰ eV the suppression mass falls to about 10⁷ M☉, so the count has to be redone across the allowed range.
- **The smallest wave halo.** The soliton core has M·r_c fixed by ħ²/(Gm²), the same scaling as the gravitational atom's Bohr radius (#4, #8, #10).

## First steps

- [ ] `halos/model.js`: the WIMP floor (dark matter inside the horizon at kinetic decoupling, plus free streaming) and the wave floor from k_J.
- [ ] Check them against published values. Numbers in this issue are from recall in a session whose literature search was exhausted, so verify them first. Hu–Barkana–Gruzinov's quoted k_J ≈ 66.5 a^¼ Mpc⁻¹ and M_J ≈ 1.5×10⁷ M☉ for 10⁻²² eV are not mutually consistent with ρ = ρ_m (a first-principles k_J is about 69 Mpc⁻¹), so state the density and the mass definition used.
- [ ] Count the nesting: extend the Aquarius subhalo mass function dN/dM ∝ M^−1.9 (Springel et al., MNRAS 391, 1685 (2008)) down to each floor. Compare with Diemand et al.'s ~10¹⁵ Earth-mass halos in the Galaxy, and with the wave suppression of Schive et al., ApJ 818, 89 (2016). Note that tidal disruption by stars and the disc makes the 10¹⁵ an upper extrapolation.
- [ ] Say which "smallest wave halo" definition is used. The Jeans mass today, the Jeans mass at matter-radiation equality, Schive's minimum halo mass and the half-mode mass differ by more than 10³.
- [ ] Say where the shapes stop being alike. Near the WIMP cutoff the first halos are reported to form steeper ρ ∝ r^−1.5 cusps rather than NFW profiles (as recalled; check Ishiyama 2014 and Delos and White 2023). Separately, small halos look alike because the CDM spectrum's slope tends to −3 on small scales: fluctuations grow only a few times over many decades of mass, so small halos form almost together.

title: Cosmic homogeneity: reproduce the scale where galaxy clustering stops looking fractal, and fix the README's range

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
## Question

At what scale does the galaxy distribution stop looking fractal? How much does the answer depend on the tracer, the redshift and the definition?

## Why it matters

The README says galaxies are spread almost evenly "beyond about 80 to 300 million parsecs (h⁻¹ Mpc, 80 to 300)" (Scrimgeour et al., 2012). Two problems:

- In Scrimgeour et al.'s abstract, 80 to 300 h⁻¹ Mpc is the range over which a fractal with D₂ < 2.97 is *excluded*; 300 h⁻¹ Mpc is just the largest scale they could probe. Their homogeneity scale is R_H = 71 ± 8, 70 ± 5, 81 ± 5 and 75 ± 4 h⁻¹ Mpc at z ≈ 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8.
- h⁻¹ Mpc is not Mpc. With h ≈ 0.67–0.70, 80 h⁻¹ Mpc is about 115–120 Mpc.

The coastline analogy also points the wrong way: a coastline's roughness stops at a small scale, the galaxies' at a large one.

## First steps

- [ ] Correlation dimension D₂(r) = 3 + 3(ξ − ξ̄)/(1 + ξ̄) from the linear ΛCDM power spectrum (Eisenstein and Hu 1998, normalised to σ₈), with bias and redshift-space distortion.
- [ ] Check it against Scrimgeour et al.'s own ΛCDM homogeneity scales (76, 78, 81, 78 h⁻¹ Mpc) and against later measurements (Hogg et al. 2005; Ntelis et al. 2017).
- [ ] Small scales: D₂ → 3 − γ ≈ 1.2 for the observed ξ = (r/r₀)^−γ, and why fits of "D ≈ 2" are an average through the crossover.
- [ ] Show how the homogeneity scale moves with bias, redshift and the 1% convention.
- [ ] Fix the README sentence and record the correction.

title: Research thread: the Witness Map, where quantum turns classical, and whether a black hole shapes wave dark matter

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: needs decision
labels.description: Waiting on a maintainer decision

body:
## What this is

An exploration from 16 Oct 2026, Aska with Claude (Anthropic). It began with an old intuition: reality might repeat itself across scales, atoms like little solar systems, solar systems like little galaxies. Pushed on with first principles and the literature, it turned into a quantitative model and one sharp open question. A pull request adding it to the site as a research page follows this issue.

No new result is claimed. The model reproduces known physics to within a factor of a few. It is not a Ledger entry: by `CONTRIBUTING.md`, the Ledger records advances that digital intelligence caused or contributed to with a checkable outcome, and this is an exploration.

## The idea in one paragraph

Ask any object one question: can it be in two places at once, a gap Δx apart? Two clocks race. The **wave clock**, m·Δx²/ħ, is how long its wave needs to spread across the gap; heavier things spread slower. The **witness clock** is how long until something in its surroundings (a scattered photon, a gas atom, its own heat glow, a black hole horizon) carries off a record of which place it is in. The **witness number W** = wave clock ÷ witness clock. Below 1 the wave wins and the object can act quantum; above 1 the witnesses win and it acts classical.

The key physical fact behind it: interference is destroyed by *which-path information*, not by the detector's push. Dürr, Nonn and Rempe tested this directly in 1998: their path marker's kick on the atoms was far too small to explain the lost interference, which they traced to the record itself ([Nature 395, 33](https://doi.org/10.1038/25653)).

## What the model shows (gap 250 nm, each object in its natural surroundings)

| Object | W | Main witness |
|---|---|---|
| Electron (lab vacuum) | ~10⁻¹³ | leftover gas |
| Rubidium atom | ~10⁻⁷ | leftover gas |
| Buckyball, C₆₀ | ~10⁻⁴ | its own heat glow |
| Giant molecule, ~2,000 atoms | ~0.05 | its own heat glow |
| Interstellar dust grain | ~10⁷ | starlight |
| Virus (air) | ~10¹⁶ | air molecules |
| Cat | ~10⁴⁸ | air molecules |
| Earth | ~10⁸¹ | sunlight |
| Milky Way | ~10¹¹⁹ | its own starlight |
| Dark matter particle (wave or heavy) | 0 | none |

1. All four objects that have been seen acting as waves in experiments land on the wave side.
2. Size enters through one door, the wave clock. Silence the witnesses and big things can cross: a virus in a 4 K vacuum scores W ≈ 0.04 at this gap, which is why a virus superposition in a cold vacuum has been proposed as an experiment.
3. Dark matter has no witnesses in this model at any gap or particle mass. That lack of witnesses is part of what makes a galaxy-sized dark matter wave possible at all ("fuzzy" or wave dark matter, de Broglie wavelength ~1 kpc for a 10⁻²² eV particle).
4. A black hole is a real witness (Danielson, Satishchandran & Wald, [arXiv:2205.06279](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06279)), but feeble. Ten horizon radii from Sagittarius A\*, a wave dark matter particle split by 1 µm waits ~10¹⁷⁰ years to be recorded. The horizon only beats ordinary witnesses for objects that are already classical.

## Checks the model passes

- Photon and gas scattering rates match the Joos–Zeh decoherence table (1985) within a factor of ~3 for the cosmic microwave background, sunlight and air.
- The horizon formula reproduces both worked examples in the Wald paper (Earth beside a Sun-mass black hole: paper ~10 µs, model ~20 µs; electron split by 1 m: paper ~10⁴³ years, model ~4×10⁴² years).
- With molecular emission calibrated 100× weaker than solid grains, a buckyball loses its wave behaviour near 2,500–3,000 K, in line with Hackermüller et al. (Nature, 2004).

## Corrections made during the exploration

Kept here so the record shows them:

- The detector's mechanical push does not explain lost interference; which-path information does (Dürr et al. 1998, above).
- "The quantum/classical line is set by witnesses, not size" was too strong. Mass matters through the wave clock.
- A quoted figure that the Big Bang afterglow localises a dust grain "in about a nanosecond" did not survive the calculation: for a 10 µm grain split by 1 mm the model gives about a millisecond.
